CS-COVERS-MULTIPLE-LO PATTERN CONFIRMED (same handling as english-language.json): Sub-Strand 1.1.1's Content Standard 1.1.1.CS.1 ('Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of binary operations, sets and binomial theorem and solve related problems in real life situations') is a single Content Standard whose 6 Learning Indicators actually span THREE different Learning Outcomes' topics (LI.1-3 = binary operations = LO.1's topic; LI.4 = set operations/properties = LO.2's topic; LI.5-6 = binomial expansion/coefficients = LO.3's topic). Per the canonical schema's one-CS-nested-under-one-LO shape, this Content Standard is nested under Learning Outcome 1.1.1.LO.1 (the first/closest topical match) with a reviewNote on the Content Standard identifying that it also covers LO.2 and LO.3 content, rather than duplicating it under three LO parents or fabricating separate Content Standards. Learning Outcomes 1.1.1.LO.2 and 1.1.1.LO.3 therefore have an empty contentStandards array with a reviewNote cross-referencing 1.1.1.CS.1. Content Standard 1.1.1.CS.2 ('numbers in relation to Surds, Indices and Logarithms') maps cleanly 1:1 onto Learning Outcome 1.1.1.LO.4 with no such issue.

FORMULA/MATHEMATICAL-NOTATION GARBLING CONFIRMED throughout, exactly as the Phase 1 inventory warned: pdftotext -layout corrupts inline mathematical notation (fractions, exponents, special operator glyphs, nCr/nPr notation) into unreadable fragments (e.g. printed binary-operation definitions render as stray isolated symbols with the actual operator/variable characters dropped or replaced). This is a source-PDF font-embedding/text-layer extraction limitation, not an extraction-tooling error on this agent's part - verbatim garbled text is preserved as extracted (per the no-silent-fix/no-fabrication rule) rather than reconstructed or guessed. Every Learning Indicator and Assessment whose worked-math content is significantly affected is flagged NEEDS_REVIEW with a reviewNote recommending human/OCR re-verification against the source PDF page directly; this affects a large proportion of nodes in this subject given how formula-heavy Additional Mathematics is - far more pervasively than any other subject extracted in this corpus so far.

GESI/SEL/National-Core-Values TABLE-WRAP-ACROSS-PAGE-BREAK pattern (same class of issue as Physics/Geography): the 4-item 'National Core Values' list under each Learning Outcome (consistently: Leadership and Respect for others' views / Diversity / Equity / Tolerance, each with topic-specific wording) is frequently split by pdftotext's column linearisation so that the 4th item ('Tolerance: ...') prints at the very top of the FOLLOWING Learning Outcome's row/page rather than under its own LO. Reconstructed per-occurrence by attributing the bleed-over 'Tolerance' bullet back to the LO whose topic-specific wording it references (confirmed reliable: each Tolerance bullet explicitly names its own LO's topic, e.g. 'as they solve problems involving properties of binary operations' unambiguously belongs to LO.1). Treated as a routine, document-wide layout-wrap issue (not flagged NEEDS_REVIEW on each individual LO) per the precedent set in geography.json/arabic.json for the same class of issue - documented once here for visibility.

learningOutcomes.description: Solve problems involving properties of binary operations.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Provide learners the opportunity to engage and participate in mathematical talk, ensuring that learners are tolerant to listen to the views and perspectives of others and use appropriate vocabulary confidently and effectively to present their ideas. Collaboration: Create an atmosphere, environment and opportunity that fosters the spirit of team success where learners understand and respect the needs, contributions, perspectives, and actions of others whilst they embark on project works, classroom activities and presentations. Critical Thinking: Provide the atmosphere, environment and opportunity for learners to observe patterns and make predictions, gather and interpret data, draw conclusions based on relevant data or personal knowledge and experience, present and receive information with others verbally, nonverbally and in writing, and put together relevant sources of information (making connections) to solve problems. Learners should compare and contrast, evaluate, analyse, generate possibilities, make inferences and interpret phenomena. (Learners respond to "why, how, when, who, what, and where" questions.) Personal and Leadership Skills: Provide the incentives for all learners to feel safe, confident and happy to participate in all activities; have all learners taste leadership roles and responsibilities whilst they work in groups; demystify the mathematics classroom and get all learners to overcome fear in the mathematics classroom. Encourage learners to keep a mathematics journal, take risks, explore and observe others they admire (inspirators and mentors) to learn from them and their actions. Creativity and Innovation: Provide a classroom atmosphere and environment that is flexible and democratic; ensure that learners reflect and visualise ideas and goals, encourage journaling and set aside a dedicated time of mindfulness each school day. Ask open-ended questions and set problem-finding contexts. Digital Literacy Skills: Provide learners the opportunity to effectively and independently use technological tools to research for information and solve problems, including drawing graphs and arithmetic computations. Strategic Competency: Conscious efforts will enable learners to collectively develop and implement innovative actions that further sustainability at the local level for application to real life.
guidance.gesi: Learners having experienced a teaching approach that ensures gender equality and social inclusion, where they work with each other in an inclusive way; cross-sharing knowledge and understanding among groups and individuals lead them to: 1. Respect individuals of different backgrounds in their groups as they solve problems involving properties of binary operations using appropriate technological tools. 2. Interrogate their stereotypes and biases about the roles and abilities of different groups as they learn how to solve problems involving properties of binary operations. 3. Examine and dispel misconceptions/myths about gender as they engage in mathematical discourse. 4. Value and promote justice in the mathematics classroom and beyond.
guidance.sel: Creating opportunities for learners to build their Social Emotional Learning Competencies - Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decisions are integrated throughout all lessons to encourage inclusion. As part of achieving each learning outcome in the SHS Additional Mathematics curriculum, the teacher should apply the Social Emotional Learning strategies to ensure that learners are: 1. Self-reflecting and developing confidence as they discuss mathematical ideas using ICT tools to promote the development of digital literacy skills. 2. Exhibiting motivation and SMART goal-setting as they use innovative ideas in solving mathematical problems. 3. Managing emotions and conflicts as they engage in collaborative group work. 4. Showing empathy and cooperation. These may be done through modelling emotional self-regulation and decision-making, the promotion of positive self-talk with self-made portraits, the creation of a vision board, creating respectful icebreakers for healthy debates, encouraging diversity presentations, and learners writing on the sequence of their activities.
guidance.gesiSelHeaderSeen: GESI1, SEL2 and Shared National Values
nationalCoreValues: Leadership and Respect for others' views: Inculcate the habit of leadership through teamwork; respect for individuals' views, beliefs and cultures through interactive and collaborative/group work as leaders in their group.
Diversity: Promote respect for divergent views to ensure inclusivity in the Additional Mathematics learning environment.
Equity: Develop fair and impartial opportunities or resources for learners without unwanted segregation or discrimination among learners as they discuss concepts based on binary operations.

Tolerance: Model tolerance among learners by creating opportunities for collaborative learning in their mixed-ability groups, emphasising differentiated instruction and assessment as they solve problems involving properties of binary operations.

contentStandards.description: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of binary operations, sets and binomial theorem and solve related problems in real life situations.
contentStandards.reviewNote: Checkpoint 6 follow-up (2026-09-29), applying the extraction phase's own pre-existing, source-verified analysis (reviewNote already present on this Content Standard from the Phase-9 extraction pass, cross-checked and confirmed correct rather than re-derived from scratch) for Sub-Strand "Number and Algebraic Patterns", SHS1: LI.1-3 (binary operations) = LO.1; LI.4 (set operations/properties) = LO.2; LI.5-6 (binomial expansion/coefficients) = LO.3. learningIndicators.description: Explain binary operations and apply that knowledge in solving related problems.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners will work in convenient groups (ability, mixed-ability, mixed gender, or pairs etc.) to identify and define binary operations over given sets and solve related problems.
Talk for Learning Approaches: Learners will brainstorm by way of think-pair-share/square and debate on sets defined by binary operations and establish the rules for such binary operations.
Experiential Learning: Learners will collaboratively engage in hands-on activity (learning by doing) to create binary operations, define them over sets and solve related problems.

Activity 1: Define and interpret Binary Operations as a rule. learningIndicators.description: Describe and interpret the characteristics of commutative, associative, distributive and closure properties of binary operations.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners will work in convenient groups (ability, mixed-ability, mixed gender, or pairs etc.) to solve problems related to identity and inverse elements and other properties of binary operations.
Talk for Learning Approaches: Learners will brainstorm through think-pair-share/square and debate to discuss and establish the identity, inverse elements, and other properties of a binary operation.

Experiential Learning: Learners will collaboratively engage in hands-on activities (learning by doing) to create binary operations, define them over sets and determine the inverse and identity elements and other properties of binary operations.

Activity 1: Identity and inverse elements of a binary operation. Use Talk for Learning Approaches, collaborative learning approaches and experiential learning approaches to investigate the relationship between inverse and identity elements of a binary operation. Small group discussions/Think-pair-share: learners investigate the elements of a binary operation to establish that the identity element e of a set S under an operation * on S exists if there is an element e such that a*e = e*a = a. Worked examples establish the identity element for operations such as a*b = a+b-ab and a*b = a+b+2 by solving for e from both the left- and right-identity equations. Similarly, learners establish that the inverse of an element a of a set S under an operation * on S is an element a^-1 in S such that a*a^-1 = a^-1*a = e, and work through worked examples finding inverse elements by solving left- and right-inverse equations.

Activity 2: Commutative, Associative, Distributive and Closure properties of binary operations. Use Talk for Learning Approaches, collaborative learning approaches and experiential learning approaches to explore the commutative, associative, distributive and closure properties of binary operations. Small group discussions/Think-pair-share: learners investigate the commutative property of a binary operation and recognise from Cayley's tables that a binary operation is commutative if the table is symmetric along its principal diagonal (worked example with a 3x3 combination table). Inter-group competition activities have learners create binary operations for each other to test for the associative property ((a*b)*c = a*(b*c) for all a,b,c in S), the distributive property (a*(b#c) = (a*b)#(a*c) for two operations * and # on S), and closure (a set S is closed under * if for any a,b in S, a*b is in S), including a worked example table for a set B={p,q,r,s} to determine whether B is closed under the operation, whether the operation is commutative, whether there is an identity element, and to find the inverse of elements of B where possible.

dokDescriptions: Level 2 Skills of conceptual understanding: A binary operation * is defined on the set S = {2,3,4,5} by a*b = a+b-ab where a,b are in S. a) Construct the table for the operation * on the set S. b) Determine whether or not the operation * is i. closed under *, ii. commutative, iii. associative and iv. distributive over # if a#b = a-3b, a,b in S.

learningIndicators.description: Determine the identity element and use it to find the inverse of a given element.
pedagogicalExemplars: Think-pair-share, Talk for Learning, Project-Based Learning. Learning Experience: Learners in pairs investigate and determine the identity element and use it to find the inverse of a given element.

Activity 1: Learners in pairs investigate the identity element of addition and multiplication and establish the definition of identity element, e.g. by solving 7-a=7, 5*a=5, 12+a=12 to conclude the identity element of addition is zero and of multiplication is one, and that an identity/neutral element leaves a combination unchanged. Through discussion, learners establish that for a binary operation *, if there exists just one element e such that a*e = e*a = a where a,e are in S, then e is called an identity element.

Activity 2: Learners in groups investigate identity elements given a combination table (worked example with set S={a,b,c,d} under an operation, establishing which element leaves each row/column unchanged).
Activity 3: Learners in groups investigate how to find the identity element when given a binary operation's definition, e.g. for a*b = a+b+5, solving a*e=a and e*a=a to find e=-5.

Activity 4: Through Talk for Learning, discuss the inverse of a binary operation and solve examples. Learners establish that an element a in S is called invertible if there exists an element a^-1 in S such that a*a^-1 = a^-1*a = e. Worked examples find the inverse (where possible) for several operation definitions, establishing that an inverse cannot be found when the identity element itself is not unique, but can be found when a unique identity element exists (worked solution shown for a*b = ab/4).

dokDescriptions: Level 1 Recall: If a*b = a+b+2, where a,b are in R, find the identity element.
Level 3 Strategic reasoning: Given that a*b = 3a+2b-ab, investigate whether the operation * has a unique identity.

learningIndicators.description: Establish the properties of operations on set, including commutative, associative, and distributive, sets algebra and apply them to solve problems.

Activity 1: Set identities and set operations. learningIndicators.description: Investigate the properties of surds and perform basic arithmetic operations on surds, including rationalisation.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners will work in convenient groups (e.g., ability, mixed-ability, mixed gender, or pairs etc.) to explore the basic properties and operations on surds in different contexts.
Talk for Learning Approaches: Learners will brainstorm using participatory activities such as think-pair-share/square and debate on various properties of surds.
Experiential Learning: Learners will work with others in groups and pairs to create surds problems involving basic operations, properties and types of surds.

Activity 1: Definition and Types of Surds. Learners identify and work to establish types of surds - recognising that a surd is a number that does not have an exact root (e.g. sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5)) and represents a number that cannot be a whole or rational number. Learners investigate and discover the types of surds: Pure Surds (a surd having only a single irrational number, e.g. sqrt(7)); Mixed Surds (a surd having a mix of a rational number and an irrational number, e.g. 5*sqrt(3)); Compound Surds (a surd composed of two surds or a surd and a rational number, e.g. 3+sqrt(10), sqrt(3)+sqrt(7)); Binomial Surd (when two surds give rise to one single surd, the resultant surd is known as a binomial surd).

Activity 2: Properties of surds. Learners establish the rules of surds, including conjugating surds - rules covering products/quotients of roots, e.g. sqrt(a*b) = sqrt(a)*sqrt(b) for a,b >= 0, and related quotient/conjugate rules [several rules printed but their exact symbolic form is corrupted in source extraction].

Activity 3: Simplification of Surds. Inter-group competition: learners from one group create surd problems whilst the other group applies properties of surds to solve them. Worked example: Simplify sqrt(108) = sqrt(36*3) = 6*sqrt(3). learningIndicators.description: Rationalise surds with binomial denominators.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning: Learners will be working in convenient groups (e.g., ability, mixed-ability, mixed gender, or pairs etc.) to solve problems involving rationalisation.

learningIndicators.description: Recollect the initial laws of indices and establish other laws for negative powers and roots.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning, Building on what others say. Learning Experience: Learners in groups explore the laws of indices.

Activity 1: Learners in pairs share ideas about indices and explain indices to their colleagues - expected responses establish that an index (indices, plural) is the power or exponent raised to a number or a variable. Learners then solve examples and use them to explore the derivation of the laws of indices.
Activity 2: Learners in their groups create and solve similar examples to establish the laws of indices.

Activity 3: Learners in their groups establish the core laws of indices - the product rule (a^m * a^n = a^(m+n), extending to a^m*a^n*a^p... = a^(m+n+p+...)), the quotient rule (a^m / a^n = a^(m-n)), the power-of-a-power rule ((a^m)^n = a^(mn)), the power-of-a-product rule, and related rules for fractional/negative exponents and roots [several rules printed but their exact symbolic form is corrupted in source extraction]. Other rules established: the negative exponent rule (a^-n = 1/a^n, extending to (a/b)^-n = (b/a)^n) and the zero power rule (a^0 = 1, where a is not 0).

learningIndicators.description: Establish the relationship between indices and logarithms and use the properties of logarithms to solve related problems in one base.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative learning, Talk for Learning, Building on what others say. Learning Experience: Learners in groups explore the relationship between indices and logarithms.

Activity 1: Relationship between indices and logarithms. Learners investigate and establish that if a^x = N, then log_a(N) = x, and the core logarithm laws: log_a(a) = 1; log_a(N^k) = k*log_a(N); log_a(MN) = log_a(M) + log_a(N); log_a(M/N) = log_a(M) - log_a(N), where M, N and P are real numbers. NB (as printed): note that log(M/N) does not equal log(M)/log(N) [note: the printed NB uses garbled notation, restated here in standard form for readability while preserving the stated logical content] and that log(M+N) does not, in general, equal log(M)+log(N).

Activity 2: Learners in mixed-ability groups solve related problems in one base. Worked example: Suppose GHS 5,000 is invested at 6% interest compounded annually; in t years the investment grows to A(t) = 5000(1.06)^t. How long will it take to accumulate GHS 15,000 in the account? Worked solution: solve 5000(1.06)^t = 15000, divide both sides by 5000 to get 1.06^t = 3, take log base 10 of both sides to get t*log(1.06) = log(3), apply the power rule, then solve t = log(3)/log(1.06) ≈ 18.85 (approximately 19 years). Further example: the value V of a Range Rover Velar that is t years old is modelled by V(t) = 25000(0.85)^t - what would the car be worth in 3 years, and in how many years will the car be worth GHS 235,000 [values as printed, some likely OCR/typing artefacts in the source itself]?

Activity 3: Learners in mixed-ability groups solve related problems in different bases, guided by the question 'What should be one important step when solving logarithm equations with different bases?' and the change-of-base rule: log_a(x) = log_b(x) / log_b(a), for x, a, b positive numbers with a, b not equal to 1.

guidance.twentyFirstCenturySkills: Communication: Provide learners with the opportunity to engage and participate in mathematical talk, ensuring that learners are tolerant and listen to the views and perspectives of others and use appropriate vocabulary confidently and effectively to present their ideas. All learners will be given the opportunity to confidently and effectively participate in different contexts to identify specific literacy skills and adopt appropriate mathematics vocabulary. Collaboration: Create an atmosphere, environment, and opportunity that fosters the spirit of team success where learners understand and respect the needs, contributions, perspectives, and actions of others while they embark on project works, classroom activities and presentations. The teacher will create an enabling environment and opportunity for learners to understand and respect the needs, perspectives, and actions of others (empathy) fostered through group/individual project works and presentations. Critical Thinking: Provide the atmosphere, environment and opportunity for learners to observe patterns and make predictions, gather and interpret data, draw conclusions based on relevant data or personal knowledge and experience, present and receive information with others verbally, nonverbally and in writing, and put together relevant sources of information (making connections) to solve problems. Learners should compare and contrast, evaluate, analyse, generate possibilities, make inferences and interpret phenomena. (Learners respond to "why, how, when, who, what, and where" questions.) Personal and Leadership Skills: Provide the incentives for all learners to feel safe, confident and happy to participate in all activities; have all learners taste leadership roles and responsibilities whilst they work in groups; demystify the mathematics classroom and get all learners to overcome fear in the mathematics classroom. Encourage learners to keep a mathematics journal, take risks, and observe others they admire (inspirators and mentors) to learn from them and their actions. Creativity and Innovation: Provide a classroom atmosphere and environment that is flexible and democratic; ensure that learners reflect and visualise ideas and goals, encourage journaling; and set aside a dedicated time of mindfulness each school day. Ask open-ended questions and set problem-finding contexts. Digital Literacy Skills: Provide learners the opportunity to effectively and independently use technological tools to research for information and solve problems, including drawing graphs and arithmetic computations. Strategic Competency: Conscious efforts will enable learners to collectively develop and implement innovative actions that further sustainability at the local level for life application. Technology Literacy Skills: Enable students to think mathematically and solve challenging problems to develop their highest potential in an information and technologically-driven world.
guidance.gesi: Learners having experienced a teaching approach that ensures gender equality and social inclusion, where they work with each other in an inclusive way; cross-sharing knowledge and understanding among groups and individuals lead them to: 1. Respect individuals of different backgrounds in their groups as they examine, analyse, determine and predict other terms in a sequence using appropriate technological tools. 2. Interrogate their stereotypes and biases about the roles and abilities of different groups as they learn about how to evaluate sequences. 3. Examine and dispel misconceptions/myths about gender as they engage in mathematical discourse. 4. Value and promote justice in the mathematics classroom and beyond.
guidance.sel: Creating opportunities for learners to build their Social Emotional Learning Competencies - Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decisions are integrated throughout all lessons to encourage inclusion. As part of achieving each learning outcome in the SHS Additional Mathematics curriculum, the teacher should apply the Social Emotional Learning strategies to ensure that learners are: 1. Self-reflecting and developing confidence as they discuss mathematical ideas using ICT tools to promote the development of digital literacy skills. 2. Exhibiting motivation and SMART goal-setting as they use innovative ideas in solving mathematical problems. 3. Managing emotions and conflicts as they engage in collaborative group work. 4. Showing empathy and cooperation. The teacher may do these through modelling emotional self-regulation and decision-making, promoting positive self-talk with self-made portraits, creating a vision board, creating respectful icebreakers for healthy debates, encouraging diversity presentations, and learners writing on the sequence of their activities.

learningIndicators.description: Recognise sequences in mathematics as an enumerated collection of objects in which repetitions are allowed and classify sequences into linear or exponential.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning Approaches, Project-based Learning, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: named pedagogies covering group problem-solving on sequences/series, brainstorming/debating the types and features of sequences, a collaborative project to develop and present a real-life-relevant sequence, hands-on creation of sequences using objects/symbols/numerals, and research inquiry into summing terms of a sequence.

Activity 1: Sequence in real life situations. Learners discuss sequences in the natural environment and create sequences using objects, symbols and numerals. Talk for Learning: learners brainstorm/debate reasons for learning about sequences (e.g. sequences and series help shape logical skills, help find the most probable terms, and equip learners with skills to find sums of things even up to infinity, useful in scientific work). Note given: 'A Sequence is any set of objects, often numbers, that follow a particular pattern infinitely. A series refers to the description of the operation that would add all of the items in a sequence.' Collaborative/Problem-based activities have learners investigate real-life patterns: stacking cups/chairs/bowls (comparing object count to height); seating around joined square tables (4, then 6, then 8 people as tables are added, noting a rectangular table variant starts at 6 seats); filling/draining a container over time; fencing and perimeter as panels are added to each side of a shape; pyramid-like patterns such as stadium/auditorium seating decreasing by a fixed amount per row; negative-number patterns such as sea-level/temperature changes over time.

Activity 2: Modelling instances of sequences. Learners work in small mixed-ability groups to model numerical and non-numerical sequences (using colours, cut-out shapes, objects, fabrics, sound, actions etc.) and describe the pattern rule, including challenging other groups to extend a pattern and write a general rule. Worked examples: a bottle-cap/pebble pattern table (pattern no. 1,2,3,4,5,6..., counts 3,6,10,...) to describe the pattern rule and derive a general rule; a squares/joints pattern table (pattern no. 1-6, squares 1,4,9,..., joints 4,9,16,...) to derive rules for the number of squares and joints in any large shape.

learningIndicators.description: Find the nth term of linear and exponential sequences.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning Approaches, Project-based Learning, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: named pedagogies covering group problem-solving, think-pair-share brainstorming on created sequences, project-based creation of a real-life-relevant sequence, hands-on activities, and inquiry into infinite sums of sequence terms.

Activity 1: Use rules to find a specified term of the sequence. Learners in pairs/groups create numeric/non-numeric sequences for other groups to identify the defining pattern, then establish the general rule for arithmetic and geometric sequences from first terms and the relationship between consecutive terms (simple recursions), identifying the first term, common difference/ratio, and nth term. Note given: an arithmetic sequence has a constant difference between consecutive terms (general rule Un = a + (n-1)d, a = first term, d = common difference, n = number of terms); a geometric sequence has each term found by multiplying the previous term by a constant (general rule Un = a*r^(n-1), a = first term, r = common ratio, n = number of terms).

Activity 2: Using a given rule or formula (input-output tables). Learners determine the first few elements of a sequence given an algebraic relationship (worked example table for Un = (1/3)(2)^(n-1), n>0, giving values 1,2,4,8,16,32 for n=1..6) and, alternatively, determine the rule for values given in a table.
Activity 3: Learners use other conventional strategies to find the nth term of a sequence.

Activity 4: Learners work in groups to describe linear and exponential sequences and use their understanding to solve real life problems. Worked example: the 2nd term of an A.P. is 15 and the 5th term is 21; find the common difference and the sum of the first 5 terms (solved via simultaneous equations a+d=15, a+4d=21, giving the sum of the first five terms as 85). Further examples: a man saving 10 pesewas on day 1, doubling daily, for 30 days (find total savings in cedis to 2 d.p.); the set of whole numbers partitioned into subsets of increasing size (1 number, then 2, then 3, ...) - find a formula in terms of n for the last member of the nth subset.

dokDescriptions: Level 2 Skills of conceptual understanding: 1. Find the 10th term of the arithmetic sequence 2, 5, 8, 11, ... 2. Given the arithmetic sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, ... find an expression for the nth term of this sequence. 3. For the geometric sequence 4, 12, 36, 108, ... find the formula for the nth term of the sequence.

Level 4 Extended critical thinking and reasoning: The set of whole numbers is partitioned into subsets, with the first number in the first subset, the next two numbers in the second subset, and the next three numbers in the third subset and so on. Find, in terms of n, a formula for the first member of the nth subset. (NB: start with a number of whole number(s) in the first partition, second partition, etc.)

learningIndicators.description: Identify Relations and Functions and describe their differences.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning Approaches, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: named pedagogies covering group problem-solving on functions/relations, brainstorming their types/features, hands-on creation of functions, and research inquiry into real-life functions.

Activity 1: Recognising relations and functions in mathematics. Learners discuss the historical development of functions (Rene Descartes in 1637 through Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Leonhard Euler, Nicolas Bourbaki, John Tate etc.) and their importance (designing machines, predicting natural disasters, curing diseases, understanding world economies, keeping aeroplanes in the air, etc.). Groups agree on and present a definition of 'function' on a poster. Worked examples have groups classify listed relations (given as ordered-pair/graph examples) as functions or not, and evaluate specific finite relations (e.g. f={(a,6),(b,4),(c,6)} from A={a,b,c} to B={4,5,6}; g={(1,d),(2,c),(1,e)} from A={1,2,3} to B={c,d,e}; a museum-to-country mapping L) for whether each is a function, justifying answers. Learners formalise the definition of function: given sets A and B, A x B is the set of all ordered pairs (a,b) with a in A, b in B; a subset of A x B is a relation; a function from A to B pairs each element of A with exactly one element of B (three equivalent phrasings given: as a pairing, as a rule/relation assigning each element to a unique element, and as a subset of the Cartesian product A x B with unique first-coordinate matching).

Activity 2: Use of mapping diagrams to establish various types of relations and connections between relations and functions, observing different graphical representations. Conclusion given: 'All functions are relations, BUT not all relations are functions. A function is a type of relation that assigns ONE output to each input.' Problem-based/Research work: learners investigate various types of functions (absolute, identity, quadratic, cubic, etc.), study the nature of their graphs, and present findings.

learningIndicators.description: Use function notation to evaluate functions for inputs in their domain and outputs in the co-domain.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning Approaches, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: named pedagogies covering group problem-solving on functions/relations, brainstorming their types/features via Think-Pair-Square, hands-on creation of functions, and inquiry into domain/range of real-life functions.

Activity 1: Determine the domain and range of functions. Learners discuss the domain and range of a function f between A and B as a non-empty relation f subset of A x B such that if (a,b) and (a,b') are both in f then b=b'. The domain of f is the set of all first elements of members of f; the range of f is the set of all second elements (given symbolically: Domain = {a : a in A; (a,b) in f for some b}, Range = {b : b in B; (a,b) in f for some a}). Worked illustration: for f(x)=x^2, inputs x=1,2,3,4,... give outputs f(x)=1,4,9,16,...; the set of output values is called the co-domain of f, and if the domain of f equals all of A, f is a function from A into B, written f: A -> B. Problem-based activity: learners investigate the domain of functions such as y=sqrt(2x-8) and share findings; learners evaluate functions for output values by substitution, e.g. given f(x)=2x-4, find f(-3). learningIndicators.description: Establish, describe and determine bijective functions and composite functions.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Talk for Learning Approaches, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: named pedagogies covering group problem-solving on functions, brainstorming bijective functions, hands-on creation of bijective functions, and investigation of one-to-one/onto/invertible functions.

Activity 1: Injective, surjective and bijective functions. Learners investigate, for two sets A and B: Definition 1 - a function f: A->B is surjective (onto) if B = range(f); Definition 2 - f is injective (one-to-one) if for all a, a' in A, f(a)=f(a') implies a=a'; Definition 3 - f is bijective if it is both surjective and injective. Learners show whether a given function is one-to-one/onto/both using mappings, diagrams and algebraic proofs. Note: a function that is both surjective and injective is said to be 'well behaved'.

Activity 2: Investigate increasing and decreasing functions, verifying graphically and algebraically: f is strictly increasing if f(x)>f(y) when x>y; strictly decreasing if f(x)<f(y) when x<y; increasing if f(x)>=f(y) when x>y; decreasing if f(x)<=f(y) when x<y. Conclusions established graphically: a function is one-to-one if it is either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing; a one-to-one function never assigns the same value to two different domain elements; for onto functions, range and co-domain are equal; if a function f is not bijective, its inverse function cannot exist as a function.

learningIndicators.description: Find the inverse of simple functions.
pedagogicalExemplars: Collaborative Learning, Experiential Learning, Problem-based Learning: learners recognise bijective functions and determine their inverse using graphic illustrations and algebraic means.

Activity 1: Inverse of a function. Note: a bijective function is also called an invertible function because it has an inverse function property; the inverse of a bijection f, denoted f^-1, assigns to y a unique x such that f(x)=y, hence f^-1(f(x))=x. Worked example: find the inverse of f(x)=2x-1 - by definition, seek a function with x as the subject; letting f(x)=y so y=2x-1, solve for x to get x=(y+1)/2, so f^-1(x)=(x+1)/2 (alternatively: swap x and y in the original equation, solve for the new y, then replace it with f^-1(x)).

Activity 1 (continued): Investigate the graphs of a function and its inverse. Learners determine domain/range of inverse functions in graphical and algebraic form; the inverse of a function is visually the original function reflected over the line y=x, and passes both the vertical and horizontal line tests. Illustrated with the graph of f(x)=2x-1 and its inverse f^-1(x)=(x+1)/2.

learningIndicators.description: Determine the composite of two given functions.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: Investigate common properties of function. Collaborative Learning: learners investigate addition and multiplication properties of functions: (f1+f2)(x) = f1(x)+f2(x); (f1*f2)(x) = f1(x)*f2(x); commutativity of function addition/multiplication; function equality (two functions are equal only when they share the same domain, co-domain, and mapping from domain to co-domain elements).

Activity 2: Composite of two functions. Learners construct two or more functions (including real-life-relevant scenarios), swap with another pair who determine the composite function, then swap back to check accuracy against the creators' intent. Learners recognise that if f is a function from A to B and g a function from B to C, the composition of f and g, denoted g∘f, is a function from A to C.

Activity 2 (continued): Investigate properties of composite functions, including: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)); f∘f^-1 = f^-1∘f = identity (f(f^-1(x))=x and f^-1(f(x))=x); if f and g are both one-to-one, f∘g is also one-to-one; if f and g are both onto, f∘g is also onto; if f and g∘f are both one-to-one, g is also one-to-one; if f and g∘f are onto, it is not necessary that g is also onto; (f∘g)^-1 = g^-1∘f^-1.

learningIndicators.description: Describe polynomial functions and perform the basic arithmetic operations on them.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: Evaluate a polynomial in function notation. Collaborative Learning: learners recall linear/non-linear function facts, examine and classify different function forms, and recognise that polynomial functions comprise combinations of constants, variables and exponents, general form f(x) = a_n*x^n + a_(n-1)*x^(n-1) + ... + a_0, where the coefficients are constants and n>=2 [exact printed form partly corrupted in extraction]. Worked example polynomial given: f(x)=4x^4-x^3-9x^2+2x-5. Note: examples of polynomial-function types are linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic and quintic; learners explore terminology (coefficient, leading coefficient, term, leading term, degree, exponents, constants).

Activity 2: Perform basic arithmetic operations on polynomial functions. Collaborative Learning, Experiential Learning, Whole class discussion, Talk for Learning Approaches, Problem-based learning: learners explore addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of polynomial functions. Worked example: given f(x)=4x^4-x^3-9x^2+2x-5 and g(x)=x^3+3x^2-2x+2, compute (f+g)(x)=4x^4-6x^2-3 and (f-g)(x)=4x^4-2x^3-12x^2+4x-7. Second worked example: given f(x)=x^2+x-6 and g(x)=x+3, compute the product f(x)*g(x)=x^3+4x^2-3x-18 and the quotient f(x)/g(x)=x-2 (using polynomial long division, generally f(x)/g(x)=q(x)+r).

Activity 3: Examine the graph of polynomial functions. Collaborative Learning, Experiential Learning, Whole class discussion, Talk for Learning Approaches, Problem-based Learning: learners identify, examine and construct graphs of polynomial functions up to degree 2 and describe their nature, then (by hand and with technology) investigate minimum/maximum values and intercepts of polynomial functions up to degree 5, swapping functions between groups/pairs to evaluate at given values and checking accuracy, with debate over the outcome.

learningIndicators.description: Use the method of completing the square to transform any quadratic equation that has the same solutions and explain how the quadratic formula is derived from this form.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: The quadratic formula and its usage. Collaborative Learning, Experiential Learning, Whole class discussion, Problem-based Learning: learners recall the general quadratic ax^2+bx+c=0 and establish the general solution x = (-b ± sqrt(b^2-4ac)) / 2a. Worked example: solve 2x^2-x-4=0 correct to 2 d.p. (a=2,b=-1,c=-4), giving x=1.69 or x=-1.19.

Learners use the method of completing the square to write ax^2+bx+c=0 in the form a(x±p)^2 ± q = 0 or a(x±p)^2 = k, where p, q/k are constants and k is the maximum/minimum value of the function, occurring at x±p=0. Worked example: express 3x^2-5x-2=0 in the form a(x±p)^2=k and state the minimum value of the function (solution given: 3(x-5/6)^2 - 49/12 = 0, minimum value -49/12).

Problem-based learning: learners use the discriminant b^2-4ac of ax^2+bx+c=0 to determine the nature of the roots: if b^2-4ac >= 0, roots are real; if b^2-4ac > 0, roots are real and different; if b^2-4ac < 0, roots are complex/imaginary; if b^2-4ac = 0, roots are real and equal (perfect square). Worked example: determine the nature of the roots of x^2-6x+4=0 (discriminant = 36-16=20>0, so real and different roots).

Activity: Use the roots (sum and product) to find other quadratic equations. Collaborative Learning: learners explore the relationship between the constants a,b,c of ax^2+bx+c=0 and the sum/product of roots, and use these relations to write quadratic equations with given roots (general form x^2-(sum of roots)x+(product of roots)=0). Worked example 1: form an equation whose roots are a and 2a (sum=3a, product=2a^2, equation x^2-3ax+2a^2=0). learningIndicators.description: Use the remainder and factor theorems to find the factors and remainders of a polynomial of degree not greater than 4.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: Use the factor and remainder theorems to solve problems of polynomial functions in context. Collaborative Learning: learners recall polynomial-function facts and recognise that dividing a polynomial by another results in dividend/divisor = quotient + remainder/divisor, i.e. dividend = divisor*quotient + remainder. For a polynomial f(x) divided by (x-a): f(x) = q(x)*(x-a) + R, where q(x) is the quotient and R the remainder. Remainder Theorem stated: given f(x) divided by (x-a), f(x)=q(x)(x-a)+R and f(a)=R. learningIndicators.description: Describe the properties of lines, including parallel, perpendicular and midpoints.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: Talk for Learning on the history of geometry, its significance and application in real life and further studies.

Activity 2: Think-pair-share to discuss straight lines, their types and characteristics. Learners establish that a straight line is formed when two points are joined by the shortest distance and can be extended forever in both directions, has no curves, is one-dimensional with no width, and that types of straight lines include horizontal, vertical, slanted, parallel and perpendicular lines.

Activity 3: Think-pair-share to discuss parallel and perpendicular lines, their characteristics and real-life examples. Parallel lines are always the same (equidistant) distance apart and never intersect (examples: railway tracks, edges of a ruler, zebra crossing markings). Perpendicular lines intersect such that all angles at the intersection are 90 degrees (examples: T-junctions on roads, corners of a football pitch).

Activity 4: Collaborative learning to find the distance between two points. Learners discover that distances are always positive, distances can only be zero if the points coincide, the distance from point A to B is the same as from B to A, and the distance between two points on a vertical/horizontal line is the difference of their shared-axis coordinates. Worked example: find the distance between the points (2,4) and (6,4) - solution: distance = 6-2 = 4.

Activity 5: Collaborative learning to discover that Pythagoras' theorem calculates the distance between two points when the interval between them is neither vertical nor horizontal, giving the distance formula d = sqrt((x2-x1)^2+(y2-y1)^2). Worked example: find the distance between A(1,2) and B(4,6) - solution: d = sqrt((4-1)^2+(6-2)^2) = 5.

Further activities (continuing under this Learning Indicator's Activity numbering, printed page 141-142): learners generalise in collaborative groups that the midpoint of a line segment is the average of the x-coordinates and the average of the y-coordinates, then solve direct and indirect questions on midpoint and distance and present their solutions to the class.

learningIndicators.description: Apply the knowledge of ratio to divide a line segment in a given ratio either internally or externally.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: learners use the Jigsaw method to investigate the division of line segments in a given ratio; group leaders discuss findings with group members.

Activity 1: Collaborative learning to link the concept of dividing by a given ratio algebraically to line segments. Worked example: dividing GHC 50 in the ratio 2:3, generalised to dividing a line segment RT at a point S such that RS:ST = 2:3.

Activity 2: Collaborative learning to discuss dividing a line segment internally in a given ratio, geometrically - group leaders lead discussion on how to geometrically locate the dividing point using a ray inclined at an acute angle, marking off equal intervals with a compass and drawing a parallel line, establishing the ratio relationship from similar triangles.

Activity 3-4: Group leaders initiate talk on dividing a line segment in a given ratio internally (and then externally) algebraically, establishing the internal-division formula (x,y) = ((m*x2+n*x1)/(m+n), (m*y2+n*y1)/(m+n)) and the corresponding external-division formula with a minus sign in place of the plus. Worked example: find the coordinates of the point dividing the line segment from (3,1) to (3,-5) in the ratio 2:1 internally (result: (3,-3)) and externally (result: (3,-11)).

learningIndicators.description: Recall the formula for finding the gradient of a line and apply it to find the equation of a straight line in various forms.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: group members recollect how to find the gradient of a line and apply it to find the equation of a line in various forms.
Activity 1: Think-pair-share on the gradient formula m = (y2-y1)/(x2-x1). Worked example: find the gradient of the line through (6,-4) and (4,2).

Activity 2: Collaborative groups find the equation of a line passing through two points, manipulating the gradient formula (using the point-gradient relationship) to deduce the equation y-y1 = m(x-x1). Worked example: find the equation of the line through (-2,4) and (4,8) - gradient found as 2/3, giving y = (2/3)x + 16/3.

Activity 3: Collaborative learning to find the equation of a line given a gradient and one point, substituting m and (x1,y1) into y-y1=m(x-x1). Worked example: find the equation of the line through (6,-2) with gradient -1/4, giving 4y+x+2=0.

Activity 4: Mixed-ability discussion of the intercept form of a line's equation; learners recollect finding x- and y-intercepts by substituting y=0/x=0 respectively. Worked example: find the x- and y-intercepts of 4y+x+2=0 (x-intercept -2, y-intercept -1/2). Learners also investigate the conditions under which the intercept form cannot be used (when the line is parallel to an axis, or passes through the origin).

Activity 4 (General/Standard Form): learners equate various equations of a line to zero and establish the general equation ax+by+c=0, investigating what happens when a=0 (horizontal line, parallel to the x-axis) or b=0 (vertical line, parallel to the y-axis), and confirm that a vertical line's equation cannot be written in the y=mx+c form, making ax+by+c=0 the most general usable form.

learningIndicators.description: Use standard algebraic manipulations to find the equation of parallel and perpendicular lines, including the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a line.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: investigate how the gradient formula applies to finding the equation of a parallel and a perpendicular line, and how to find the equation of a perpendicular bisector.

Activity 1: Think-pair-share to find the gradient of a parallel line - learners recollect that parallel lines have the same gradient. Worked example: find the gradients of lines through (2,3)/(5,6) and (-1,4)/(5,10), confirming both gradients equal 1, so the lines are parallel.

Activity 2: Think-pair-share on the equation of a parallel line, applying the parallel-gradient property and point-gradient equation. Worked example: find the equation of the line parallel to y=-2x+6 through (1,10) - solution y=-2x+12.

Activity 3: Mixed-ability groups find the gradient of a perpendicular line, establishing that if one line's gradient is m, a perpendicular line's gradient is -1/m (equivalently, the product of perpendicular gradients is -1). Worked example: find the gradients of two lines through given point pairs and confirm they are perpendicular (gradients 5 and -1/5).

Activity 4: Think-pair-share to deduce the equation of a perpendicular line using the perpendicular-gradient relationship and point-gradient equation. Worked example: find the equation of the line through (1,3) perpendicular to y=2x+1 - solution y = -x/2 + 7/2.

Activity 5: Mixed-ability discussion of the equation of a perpendicular bisector, combining the midpoint formula and the perpendicular-gradient relationship. Worked example: find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (-4,8) and (0,-2) - midpoint (-2,3), perpendicular-bisector gradient 2/5, final equation 5y-2x-19=0.

learningIndicators.description: Deduce the shortest distance between a point and a line and use the knowledge of intercepts and right-angled triangles to find the perpendicular distance from an external point to a line.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: investigate the shortest distance between a point and a line, and between two lines, through real-life measuring activities in the classroom and around the school.
Activity 1: Collaborative groups investigate the shortest distance between a point and a line, establishing that the shortest distance from a point to a line is the perpendicular distance.

Activity 2: Learners derive/apply the perpendicular-distance formula d = |a*x1+b*y1+c| / sqrt(a^2+b^2) for a point (x1,y1) and a line ax+by+c=0, recognising the numerator as the line's equation evaluated at the point and the denominator as the Pythagorean hypotenuse-length term. Worked example: find the perpendicular distance from (1,9) to the line -5x+12y+13=0.

Activity 3: Learners apply the equation-of-a-line and perpendicular-distance knowledge to an application question - given a point and two other points defining a line, first find the line's equation, then apply the perpendicular-distance formula. Worked example: find the perpendicular distance from (-1,-7) to the line through (6,-4) and (9,-5) (line equation found as x+3y+6=0).
Activity 4: Learners find the distance between two parallel lines, established as the perpendicular distance from any point on one line to the other line.

learningIndicators.description: Recognise and explain various forms of vectors and apply the knowledge to find unit vectors.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: a mixed-ability group conceptualises the idea of vectors, performs algebraic manipulations on vectors, and interprets them geometrically.
Activity 1: Think-pair-share to recollect the definition of a vector, vector notation, and types/examples of vectors.

Activity 2: Collaborative learning to express vectors in a Cartesian plane, in column form and in i-j component form, and to calculate a vector's magnitude. Worked example: express the vectors from the origin to (2,4) and to (-3,7) in column form. Learners also express vectors in magnitude-and-direction (bearing) form, e.g. a location 40 metres away on a bearing of 150 degrees is written as (40, 150 degrees), and practise estimating and expressing classmates' seating positions relative to the teacher's table in this form.

Activity 3: Collaborative groups identify parallel vectors from a set of given vectors and generalise that two vectors are parallel when one can be expressed as a scalar multiple of the other. Worked example: given five vectors, identify which pairs are parallel by inspecting scalar-multiple relationships between their components.

Further activities (Learning Experience on resultant vectors via polygon laws of addition): collaborative groups discuss and diagram the triangle law of addition, then the parallelogram law of addition and polygon law of addition, and represent vector subtraction and scalar multiplication diagrammatically. Learners perform algebraic manipulations on vectors - worked example: given vectors a=(3,-4) and b=(5,0), with p=(1/4)(a+b) and q=(1/2)(a-b), show that |p+q| = |p-q| (solution confirms both magnitudes equal sqrt(10)).

learningIndicators.description: Describe and interpret the meaning of the limit of a function through graphical and algebraic approaches.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups consolidate understanding of the concept of limits in mathematics and daily life using both algebraic and graphical means.

Activity 1: demonstrate the concept of limits using algebraic/graphical means. Worked examples: investigate and interpret the limit of f(x) as x approaches 2 using a graph, and using a table of values for f(x)=x^2 to show f(x) gets closer to 4 as x approaches 2.
Activity 2: investigate the behaviour of a function over different input-value intervals and share observations (worked example uses a piecewise function graphed in GeoGebra over several intervals).
Activity 3: think-pair-share within and across groups to investigate and discuss the value a function approaches as x approaches -7 on a given graph.

Extension note: the concept of limit underlies calculus, illustrated via inscribing polygons of increasing side-count in a circle - as the number of sides n tends to infinity, the limit of the inscribed polygon's area and perimeter equal the circle's area and circumference respectively.

learningIndicators.description: Classify left-hand and right-hand limits algebraically and with the aid of technology where available or through any creative means.
pedagogicalExemplars: Group discussion / Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups discuss the meaning of approaching a number on a real number line from the left or right.

Activity 1: represent left- and right-hand limits algebraically and graphically. Worked examples (using a reference graph): the value f(x) approaches as x approaches -7 differs from the left (4) versus the right (2), introducing one-sided limit notation; the generalisation that lim_{x->c} f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x gets close to c from both sides; determining whether a limit exists (left-hand limit equals right-hand limit) versus does not exist (they differ); comparing the limit of a function at a point with the function's actual value at that point (these need not be equal).

Mini-project: construct a table and graph, using technology, to investigate the behaviour of f(x)=1/(x-2)^2 as x approaches 2 from the left (using input values 1.97, 1.988, 1.9998) and from the right (2.03, 2.002, 2.0001), introducing the idea of unbounded behaviour (a function growing without bound/to infinity at the limit point).

Limit Properties (established and applied via worked examples, Examples 6-8): for a constant k, lim[k*f(x)] = k*lim f(x); lim[f(x)]^n = [lim f(x)]^n; lim[f(x)+g(x)] = lim f(x) + lim g(x); lim[f(x)-g(x)] = lim f(x) - lim g(x); lim[f(x)*g(x)] = lim f(x) * lim g(x); lim[f(x)/g(x)] = lim f(x) / lim g(x) provided lim g(x) is not 0; the limit of a polynomial function at c equals the function evaluated at c; the limit of a rational function at c (where the denominator is nonzero at c) equals the function evaluated at c.

Determinate vs Indeterminate Forms: an undefined expression is a determinate form if it evaluates to a single value or infinity, and an indeterminate form if it does not - the indeterminate forms listed are 0/0, infinity/infinity, 0*infinity, infinity-infinity, 1^infinity, infinity^0 and 0^0; learners are told to recognise and resolve these without necessarily using L'Hopital's Rule.

Worked Example 9: evaluate limits that initially yield the 0/0 indeterminate form by algebraic manipulation - one example resolved by rationalising the numerator (a surd expression divided by x), another by factoring numerator and denominator to cancel a common factor (a quadratic-over-quadratic expression), each concluding with a specific finite numeric limit value.

Activity 2 (limits at infinity): worked example evaluating the limit as x approaches infinity of (x+1)/(x-1), concluding the limit equals 1 by dividing numerator and denominator by the highest power of x; a further limit-at-infinity example involving a quadratic expression is set up but its worked solution is not legibly captured in this extraction pass (see reviewNote).

learningIndicators.description: Distinguish between continuous and discontinuous functions near an input value on its domain and investigate them with the use of technology or any other means appropriate.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups investigate and classify various functions into continuous and discontinuous functions and relate these to things around them.

Activity 1: identify point(s)/interval(s) of continuity or discontinuity of a function on a graph and algebraically. Definition given: a function f is continuous at a point a if lim_{x->a} f(x) = f(a). Theorem (3 conditions for continuity at a): f(a) is defined; the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is defined (left and right limits are the same); and the limit equals f(a). Worked examples: identify discontinuity points from a reference graph (discontinuous at x=-7 and x=-4, due to jumps); determine whether several given functions (a linear function, a rational function, an absolute-value function) are continuous at x=2.
Activity 2: use GeoGebra/technology to investigate and identify points of discontinuity of a given rational function.

NB (conceptual notes): the value f(c) plays no role in the definition of the limit of f(x) as x tends to c - f need not even be defined at c; a definition of 'limit' requiring f to be defined at c would not apply to many important applications, since the limit represents what we anticipate f(x) will equal near x=c, not necessarily what f(c) actually equals. An analogy is given of driving along a road where visibility is limited: we anticipate the road continues as seen (continuous) unless something (e.g. a damaged bridge) breaks that expectation (discontinuous).

learningIndicators.description: Use the limits of a function to find its derivative.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups investigate how the limit of a function relates to its derivative.

Activity 1: investigate algebraically and graphically how the limit of a function relates to its derivative, motivated by finding a runner's instantaneous speed from a distance-time film (average speed over [t,u] = (s(u)-s(t))/(u-t), leading intuitively to instantaneous velocity as u approaches t). Different derivative notations are introduced: f'(x), dy/dx, df/dx. The slope of the tangent line is identified as the instantaneous rate of change of f at x.

Activity 2: brainstorm to establish, from the runner/tangent-line context, the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient: f'(x) = lim_{h->0} [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h. Procedure: find f(x+h); form the difference quotient; simplify it; take the limit as h approaches 0.

Worked Example 1 (first-principles differentiation): find the derivatives of f(x)=2x^2, f(x)=6x+4 and f(x)=3x^2-6x+7 using first principles - full worked solution shown for f(x)=2x^2, giving f'(x)=4x.

Worked Example 2 (continuous but not differentiable): use limits to show f(x)=|x| is not differentiable at x=0, because the left-hand difference-quotient limit is -1 while the right-hand limit is +1, which disagree (illustrated with a graph, Fig. 4). NB: all differentiable functions are continuous, but not all continuous functions are differentiable - differentiability is a stronger condition than continuity.

Worked Example 3: identify, from a given graph (Fig. 5), the x-values where the function is not differentiable, distinguishing points that are also discontinuous from points that are continuous but not differentiable (e.g. corners).

Activity 4 (Generalisation - power rule): establish the general derivative formula for f(x)=x^n (n a natural number) using the binomial expansion of (x+h)^n, arriving at f'(x) = n*x^(n-1). A further worked example applies differentiation rules (power rule and linear combination) to a list of polynomial functions, though only the first few derivatives in the list were legibly captured (see reviewNote).

Derivative of sine and cosine (Theorem): d/dx[sin(x)] = cos(x) and d/dx[cos(x)] = -sin(x), proved using the compound-angle expansion of sin(x+h) and the two standard limits lim_{h->0} [cos(h)-1]/h = 0 and lim_{h->0} sin(h)/h = 1; learners are then asked to establish the cosine-derivative result similarly in pairs.

learningIndicators.description: Generalise the behaviour of a moving object along a path or curve.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups investigate the behaviour of a moving object along a path or curve and provide generalisations for whole-class discussion.
Activity 1: think-pair-share - draw a graph and investigate the behaviour of an object moving along it with respect to derivatives.

Activity 2: in pairs, find the domain value(s)/interval(s) where a function f increases, decreases or shows no change as x increases. Worked Examples 1-3: for f(x)=3x+4, f'(x)=3>0 so f increases; for f(x)=-5x+4, f'(x)=-5<0 so f decreases; for f(x)=7 (constant), f'(x)=0, momentarily at rest. General rule established: f increases where f'(x)>0, decreases where f'(x)<0, and is momentarily at rest where f'(x)=0.

Worked Example 4 (fuller applied problem): for f(x)=2x^3-9x^2-24x+56, find f'(x)=6x^2-18x-24; solve f'(x)=0 by factoring to (x-4)(x+1)=0, giving critical points x=4 and x=-1 where f is momentarily at rest; partition the real line into (-infinity,-1), (-1,4) and (4,infinity); test a sample value of f'(x) in each interval (x=-2 gives f'=36>0 so increasing on (-infinity,-1); x=3 gives f'=-26<0 so decreasing on (-1,4); x=5 gives f'=36>0 so increasing on (4,infinity)). NB: a graphical approach may also be used to confirm these results.

learningIndicators.description: Use knowledge of differentiation to determine the equation of tangents and normal to curves at a given point.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups explore ways of finding the equation of the tangent to a curve.

Activity 1: think-pair-share, using previous knowledge of finding the equation of a line, to investigate and discuss how to determine the equation of a line tangent to a curve. Worked example: find the equation of the tangent line to y=6x^2 at the point (1,6) - step 1, differentiate to get dy/dx=12x, so the slope at (1,6) is 12; step 2, use the point-gradient equation to get y=12x-6.

Activity 2: group work using the same previous knowledge to find the equation of the line normal to y=6x^2 at (1,6), using the fact that the normal's gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient.
Note: learners are reminded that a tangent line to a circle is always perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, and touches the circle at only that one point.

learningIndicators.description: Apply differentiation to find the rate of change.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups explore ways of finding the rate of change of a given function or phenomenon at certain points.

Activity 1: think-pair-share, using previous knowledge of finding slope between two points, to find the rate of change at a point. Worked Example 1: a dropped ball has height h(t)=100-4.9t^2 metres, t seconds after release - find the average speed between t=2 and t=3 (height falls from 80.4m to 55.9m, average speed 24.5 m/s), then use the difference quotient (h(2)-h(2+dt))/dt as dt shrinks toward 0 to find the exact (instantaneous) speed at t=2 as 19.6 m/s.

Further worked example (applied context): during the COVID-19 pandemic in Accra, the number of persons with COVID-19 at time t days is modelled by P(t)=45t^2-t^3 (0<=t<=50). Find the rate of spread at t=10 (derivative P'(t)=90t-3t^2, giving P'(10)=600 people/day) and find the time(s) at which the rate of spread is 600 people/day (solving 90t-3t^2=600 gives t=10 or t=20).

Worked Example 2: for f(x)=x^2, calculate the average rate of change over the intervals [1,2], [1,1.1] and [1,1.01] (values 3, 2.1, 2.01 respectively, using the ratio (f(1+dx)-f(1))/dx), then determine the instantaneous rate of change at x=1 as f'(1)=2*1=2.

Worked Example 3 (introduced, solution not captured in this extraction pass): a production function p(x) gives units of goods produced when employing x units of labour; given p(4000)=200 and p'(4000)=4, estimate the additional units of goods produced for one additional unit of labour, an additional 1/4 unit of labour, and one less unit of labour.

learningIndicators.description: Calculate measures of central tendencies (mode, mean and median) for a given data by formulas or other techniques and establish which is appropriate to report on a given data.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups discuss measures of central tendency, how to calculate them for grouped and ungrouped data, and which is appropriate to report for given data.

Activity 1: recollect mode (most frequent value), median (middle value when data is ordered - or the average of the two middle values when the count is even) and mean (sum of values divided by count) for raw data, with worked examples (e.g. mode/median/mean of an 11-value data set; mean of Akua's 7 exam scores, giving 79.6).
Activity 2: extend measures of central tendency to ungrouped data with repeated values.

Activity 3: extend to grouped data - construct a frequency table with class boundaries/midpoints, then compute the mean via the direct-mean formula (mean = sum of frequency*midpoint / sum of frequency, worked example giving a mean mass of 64kg for 40 students' grouped mass data), the mode by inspection and by the grouped-mode formula (mode = lower boundary of modal class + [d1/(d1+d2)]*class width, where d1/d2 are the modal class's frequency excess over the adjacent lower/higher classes respectively; worked example gives mode approx. 61-62), the median via the grouped-median formula (median = lower boundary of median class + [(n/2 - cumulative frequency before median class)/frequency of median class]*class width; worked example gives median 62.3), and the assumed-mean method (actual mean = assumed mean + sum(f*d)/sum(f), where d is each class midpoint's deviation from the assumed mean; worked example gives assumed-mean result 62.4).
Activity 3 (research): research how to select an appropriate assumed mean and share findings with the class.

learningIndicators.description: Work out simple measures of dispersion (range, quartile and, inter-quartile, etc.) for raw data and interpret them in context.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: mixed-ability groups discuss estimating measures of dispersion.

Activity 1: estimate quartiles of given data using a cumulative frequency curve - the lower quartile corresponds to the 25th percentile, the median to the 50th percentile, the upper quartile to the 75th percentile, and the interquartile range = upper quartile - lower quartile. Worked example: using the same 50-student mark-distribution data as LI.5's cumulative-curve example, find the median, semi-interquartile range and the pass mark if 30% of students passed.

Activity 2: work out standard deviation - a statistic describing the spread of data around the mean (higher standard deviation = more spread; data close to the mean gives a lower standard deviation). Formulas given for standard deviation of raw data (sqrt(sum((x-mean)^2)/n)), ungrouped data with a frequency column (sqrt(sum(f*x^2)/sum(f) - mean^2)), and grouped data (sqrt(sum(f*x^2)/sum(f) - (sum(f*x)/sum(f))^2)). Worked example: standard deviation of 8 students' ages (14,14,15,15,12,11,13,10), mean 13, giving standard deviation approximately 1.7.

Activity 3: work out variance, established as the square of the standard deviation. Worked example: construct a frequency distribution table for 50 citizens' ages and calculate the standard deviation (approx. 15.33 years, per the worked solution) and variance (approx. 235.04) of the distribution.
Activity 4: research how to interpret measures of dispersion with respect to real data and present findings.

learningIndicators.description: Use the fundamental counting principle to identify and determine the number of ways an event can occur.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: learners establish different ways of counting, inquire into what happens when elements are repeated in an arrangement, and explore different ways of counting.

Activity 1: think-pair-share to establish the fundamental counting principle - if a task can be accomplished in m different ways and a following second task in n ways, the two tasks together can be accomplished in m*n ways. Worked examples: Akwesi has 5 pairs of trousers and 8 shirts, giving 5*8=40 outfit combinations; an eatery with 3 corn dishes and 4 drinks giving 12 meal-with-drink combinations; forming 3-digit numbers with distinct digits from {1,2,3,4,5}, giving 5*4*3=60 possibilities.

Activity 2 (arrangements with repetition): problem-based learning to investigate what happens when elements can repeat. Worked examples: how many 3-digit numbers can be formed from digits 1-5 if repetition is allowed; how many WASSCE-style ID numbers (one capital letter followed by a 3-digit number, digits may repeat) can be formed.

learningIndicators.description: Discuss the concepts of permutation and combination and use them to solve real life problems.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: learners discuss types/features of permutations (circular arrangements, identical elements, etc.) and what happens with ordered/unordered and special arrangements.

Activity 1 (ordered arrangements): learners establish that permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects (e.g. APC differs from PAC), working through examples such as the 6 possible finishing-order arrangements of 3 race contestants (initials E, A, M). Worked example: Kweku has 4 different books on his shelf - the number of orders to arrange them is 4*3*2*1=24, introducing factorial notation n! for the number of permutations of n objects.

Activity 2 (permutation formula): learners establish the permutation formula for selecting r items from n where order matters: nPr = P(n,r) = n!/(n-r)! = n(n-1)(n-2)...[n-(r-1)]. Worked example: evaluate 5P3 = 5!/(5-3)! = 60.

Activity 3 (permutation with repeated objects): learners establish that the number of arrangements of n objects where groups of r1, r2, ... rk are identical is n!/(r1!*r2!*...*rk!). Worked example: arrangements of the letters of 'SECRETS' (7 letters, S and E each repeated twice) = 7!/(2!*2!) - printed working shows an apparent typo using n=5 rather than 7, giving a stated answer of 30 ways (see reviewNote).

Activity 4 (circular permutations): through role play, learners discover that the number of ways of arranging n objects in a circle is (n-1)!. Worked example: 6 people seated at a circular table can be arranged in (6-1)!=5!=120 ways.

learningIndicators.description: Distinguish between the concepts of permutation and combination and establish the relationship between them.
pedagogicalExemplars: Learning Experience: learners discuss types/features of permutations (as in LI.2) and what happens with ordered/unordered and special arrangements.

Activity 1 (ordered vs unordered): learners distinguish ordered choices (order matters, e.g. permutations) from unordered choices (order doesn't matter, e.g. APC and PAC are the same set), then establish the combination formula: nCr = C(n,r) = n!/[r!(n-r)!]. Worked examples: a committee of 3 from a team of 8 can be formed in 8C3 = 8!/[3!(8-3)!] = 56 ways; drawing a set of 3 cubes from 6 differently-coloured cubes in a bag (nCr application, solution not fully captured).

Activity 2 (combination as counting): learners combine the fundamental counting principle with the combination formula. Worked example: a committee of 2 women and 1 man from 4 women and 2 men - select 2 women in 4C2 ways and 1 man in 2C1 ways, giving 4C2*2C1 = 6*2 = 12 ways.

Activity 3 (relationship between combination and permutation): learners establish that nCr = n!/[r!(n-r)!] = nPr/r!, and use it to solve problems. Worked example: find n given ratio equations such as nP3/nC4=24/5 and nC5/nP4=1/4 (solutions not captured in this extraction pass, see reviewNote).

Activity 1 (relative frequencies of events): groups perform experiments using coins, dice, playing cards, etc. for about 10 trials each and record findings. Worked examples: given a table of 13 (then 26) coin-toss trial outcomes, calculate the relative frequency of heads/tails after each trial and after the full experiment (e.g. relative frequency of heads after 13 trials = 6/13 = 0.46), and compare the observed relative frequency to the theoretical probability, including graphing how relative frequency varies over the trials.

learningIndicators.description: Generate the terms of a recurrence sequence and find an explicit formula for the sum of the sequence.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1: revise facts about arithmetic and geometric sequences (nth term, means, similarities/differences, sequences that are neither AP nor GP).
Activity 2: use summation (sigma) notation to generate terms of a series from its general term.

Activity 3 (method of undetermined coefficients): find the sum of the first n terms of a series by equating it to a polynomial form an+bn^2+... and solving for the constants. Worked example: derive the sum of the first n natural numbers, sum = n(n+1)/2, via this method; a further example applies partial fractions to evaluate a sum involving (2n-1)(2n+1) in the denominator.

Activity 4 (sum of AP and GP): establish and apply the AP sum formulas Sn=(n/2)(a+l) and Sn=(n/2)[2a+(n-1)d], and the GP sum formulas Sn=a(1-r^n)/(1-r) for r<1 (or a(r^n-1)/(r-1) for r>1). Worked examples: sum of all even integers from 250 to 350 (=15,000 using a=250,l=350,n=50); a pyramid-of-milk-tins problem (bottom layer 25 tins, each layer 2 fewer) as an AP-sum application; evaluating a geometric series like 1-2/3+4/9-8/27+... and summation-notation series.

Activity 5 (convergence/divergence of a series): investigate whether an infinite series converges by examining its partial sums. Worked example: the series sum of 1/2^n from n=1 (a GP with a=1/2, r=1/2<1) has partial sums approaching 1, illustrating convergence to the infinite sum a/(1-r); the concept of partial sums Sn and the limit L (the sum of a convergent infinite series) is introduced, with a divergence example (a series with |r|>1) also posed.

learningIndicators.description: Find the factors and zeros of a polynomial function using conventional and personal strategy.
pedagogicalExemplars: Activity 1 (factoring/solving/roots/zeros terminology): establish that factors of a polynomial multiply to give that polynomial (e.g. x^2+2x-15=(x-3)(x+5)); solving a polynomial equation by setting it to zero and factoring gives its roots/solutions, also called its zeros.

Activity 2 (graphical zeros): establish that a polynomial's real roots/zeros are the x-intercepts of its graph. Worked example: for f(x)=x^2+2x-15, factors (x+5)(x-3), roots x=-5,3, zeros at (-5,0) and (3,0).

Activity 3 (Rational Zeros Theorem): every rational zero p/q of a polynomial with integer coefficients has p as a factor of the constant term and q as a factor of the leading coefficient. Worked examples: list all possible rational zeros of f(x)=6x^4+7x^3-4 by the theorem; find all real zeros of P(x)=2x^4+x^3-6x^2-7x-2 using synthetic division to test candidate roots, factoring fully as (x+1)^2(x-2)(2x+1), giving zeros -1 (double), 2 and -1/2.

Activity 4 (Descartes' Rule of Signs): the number of positive real zeros equals the number of sign changes in P(x) or less by an even number; similarly for negative real zeros using P(-x). Worked example: for P(x)=6x^3+17x^2-31x-12, determine the possible counts of positive/negative real zeros (1 positive; 0 or 2 negative, giving 1 or 3 total real zeros).

Activity 5 (Fundamental Theorem of Algebra): every degree-n polynomial equation with complex coefficients has exactly n roots in the complex numbers (not all necessarily distinct real intercepts) - illustrated by comparing a degree-3 polynomial with 3 real x-intercepts to one with only 1 real x-intercept (the other 2 roots being complex). Further worked example: fully factor P(x)=4x^5-324x, finding zeros 0, 3, -3, 3i, -3i (each multiplicity 1).

Activity 6 (Complex Conjugates Theorem): non-real roots of a real-coefficient polynomial occur in conjugate pairs. Worked example: find all roots of P(x)=x^3-5x^2-7x+51 given one root is 4-i - the conjugate 4+i is also a root, their product factor is x^2-8x+17, and dividing P(x) by this factor gives the third (real) root x=-3.

Activity 7 (Linear and Quadratic Factors Theorem): every real-coefficient polynomial factors into linear and irreducible-quadratic real factors (or fully into linear complex factors). Worked example: factor P(x)=x^4+2x^2-63 both ways.
